title: Gesture-controlled wheelchair with hurdle detection
highlights: X on PA1 and Y on PA2 are read through the 10-bit ADC; threshold bands decide forward, back, left, right or stop.
The motor driver is on PORTB bits 4-7, and a 16x2 LCD on PORTC shows the live readings.
An IR obstacle input on PORTD stops the chair, shows "OBJ DETECTED" and backs away.
A UART receive interrupt at 9600 baud, with the rest of the control loop in polled C.
summary: ATmega32 firmware that turns hand tilt into wheelchair motion. A two-axis MEMS accelerometer is read through the ADC, and an IR obstacle input overrides the motors. Team project.

details.label: How a tilt becomes a command
details.body: The accelerometer outputs an analog voltage per axis, which the ADC converts to a 10-bit number. A resting hand sits near the middle. A Y reading below 285 means forward and above 385 means backward; an X reading above 385 means left and below 285 means right; X between 321 and 340 counts as stop. Dead bands between the thresholds keep small tremors from moving the chair.

details.label: Safety override
details.body: The obstacle sensor is read on PORTD. When it triggers, the firmware stops the motors whatever the tilt says, shows "OBJ DETECTED" on the LCD and drives backward to clear the obstacle. The obstacle check outranks the gesture input.

details.label: Hardware
details.body: The motor driver takes direction bits from PORTB bits 4-7. The 16x2 LCD on PORTC shows the readings so the thresholds could be tuned by watching the numbers. A UART receive interrupt runs at 9600 baud; the rest of the loop uses polled delays.
